idiom_name: request.user / scope['user'] set by framework middleware, with contextvars.ContextVar for code off the request path
implementation_notes: Python's dominant realization is framework-owned: Django's AuthenticationMiddleware attaches request.user to every request and authenticate()/login() are the documented seam, while Starlette's AuthenticationMiddleware writes scope['user'] and Flask-Login stores the user on the request-scoped g object - guards that receive the request read the principal directly and no container class is needed. For code that must reach the principal without the request - helpers, tasks spawned from a request, async libraries - the ambient carrier is contextvars.ContextVar, which the standard library recommends over threading.local for concurrent and asynchronous code and which asyncio copies into each task. Keep the ContextVar at module level, set it in one middleware and reset the token in a finally block; a classic context object is justified only when several attributes travel together, and then it should be one immutable value rather than several variables.
pitfalls: A module-level mutable global (or an attribute on a shared service object) is shared across requests in a threaded server - use the request object or a ContextVar instead.
ContextVar values are copied per context: a task created before set() never sees the value, and reset(token) must run in the same context that called set().
Django's request.user is lazy and anonymous users are real objects: reading it may hit the database and is_authenticated must be tested explicitly rather than relying on truthiness.
